william-henry-harrison.name: William Henry Harrison
william-henry-harrison.summary: Ninth U.S. president (1773–1841), who died just 31 days into office, the shortest term of any president; earlier a military officer nicknamed 'Old Tippecanoe' for his 1811 victory over Tecumseh's confederacy.

martin-van-buren.name: Martin Van Buren
martin-van-buren.summary: Eighth president of the United States (1837–1841) who co-founded the Democratic Party with Andrew Jackson and served as his vice president from 1833 to 1837.

whig-party-united-states.name: Whig Party
whig-party-united-states.summary: A major US political party of the 1830s-1850s formed in opposition to President Andrew Jackson, favoring a protective tariff, internal improvements, and a national bank.

threshing-machine.name: Threshing machine
threshing-machine.summary: A piece of farm equipment that separates grain from stalks and husks by beating the plant, replacing laborious hand-threshing with flails.

nathaniel-parker-willis.name: Nathaniel Parker Willis
nathaniel-parker-willis.summary: An American writer, poet and editor (1806–1867) who became the highest-paid magazine writer of his day, working with figures such as Edgar Allan Poe.

pork-roll.name: Pork roll
pork-roll.summary: A processed pork product developed in 1856 in Trenton, New Jersey, still called 'Taylor Ham' in the northern part of the state.

lutefisk.name: Lutefisk
lutefisk.summary: A traditional Nordic dish of dried whitefish, usually cod, cured in lye until gelatinous, historically served at Christmas feasts in Norway, Sweden and Finland.

egg-coffee.name: Egg coffee
egg-coffee.summary: Vietnamese drink made with egg yolks, sugar, condensed milk and coffee, originating in Hanoi and associated with the Giang Café.

nez-perce.name: Nez Perce
nez-perce.summary: An Indigenous people of the Columbia River Plateau in the Pacific Northwest, dominant in the region for centuries and known for breeding the Appaloosa horse after acquiring horses in the 18th century.

cree.name: Cree
cree.summary: A North American Indigenous people numbering over 350,000, forming one of Canada's largest First Nations groups, with homelands stretching from Quebec across the Canadian Prairies to British Columbia.

coast-salish-peoples.name: Coast Salish peoples
coast-salish-peoples.summary: A group of related Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast, living across British Columbia, Washington and Oregon with many distinct nations, languages and cultures.

blackfoot-confederacy.name: Blackfoot Confederacy
blackfoot-confederacy.summary: An alliance of related Indigenous peoples of the northern Great Plains in the US and Canada, once nomadic bison hunters who used horses and firearms from the 1700s to expand their territory.

lewis-and-clark-expedition.name: Lewis and Clark Expedition
lewis-and-clark-expedition.summary: A US expedition (1804-1806) commissioned by President Thomas Jefferson after the Louisiana Purchase, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, that crossed the western continent to the Pacific Ocean and back.

hudson-river-school.name: Hudson River School
hudson-river-school.summary: A mid-19th-century American art movement of landscape painters, influenced by Romanticism, whose early works depicted the Hudson River Valley and surrounding mountains.

academic-art.name: Academic art
academic-art.summary: A style of painting and sculpture shaped by European art academies from 16th-century Italy to the early 20th century, peaking in the 19th century with an emphasis on classical tradition.

louisiana-purchase.name: Louisiana Purchase
louisiana-purchase.summary: 1803 sale of a huge stretch of French-claimed land west of the Mississippi to the United States for $15 million, roughly doubling the young country's size.

armory-show.name: Armory Show
armory-show.summary: 1913 exhibition in New York, Chicago and Boston that introduced Americans to European avant-garde art such as Fauvism and Cubism, becoming a landmark in American art history.

george-catlin.name: George Catlin
george-catlin.summary: American lawyer, painter, author and traveler (1796–1872) who specialised in portraits of Native Americans, traveling to the American West five times during the 1830s.

george-caleb-bingham.name: George Caleb Bingham
george-caleb-bingham.summary: American painter (1811–1879), known in his lifetime as 'the Missouri artist,' celebrated for genre scenes of westward expansion and life along the Mississippi and Missouri rivers.

second-empire-style.name: Second Empire style
second-empire-style.summary: An eclectic French architectural and decorative style flourishing under Napoleon III from 1852 to 1870, blending historical elements with modern materials like iron and glass.

folk-victorian.name: Folk Victorian
folk-victorian.summary: A plainer, less ornate branch of Victorian architecture built in the US and Europe mostly from 1870 to 1910, marked by decorative trim on simple, regularly planned homes.

richardsonian-romanesque.name: Richardsonian Romanesque
richardsonian-romanesque.summary: A style of Romanesque Revival architecture named after American architect Henry Hobson Richardson (1838–1886), drawing on 11th- and 12th-century French, Spanish and Italian Romanesque features, popular in the late 1800s.

shingle-style-architecture.name: Shingle style
shingle-style-architecture.summary: An American architectural style, popular in New England, using plain shingled surfaces and horizontal massing inspired by colonial buildings, unlike more ornamented Victorian styles.

jacob-wrey-mould.name: Jacob Wrey Mould
jacob-wrey-mould.summary: British architect, illustrator, and musician (1825–1886) noted for his work on New York City's Central Park and for bringing British High Victorian style to the US.

building-magazine.name: The Builder
building-magazine.summary: British trade magazine launched in 1843, the only UK title covering the entire building industry; it was renamed Building in 1966.

massachusetts-museum-of-contemporary-art.name: MASS MoCA (Arnold Print Works)
massachusetts-museum-of-contemporary-art.summary: A converted textile factory complex in North Adams, Massachusetts, run by the Arnold Print Works from 1860 to 1942, later reopened in 1999 as one of the largest contemporary art museums in the US.

painted-ladies.name: Painted Ladies
painted-ladies.summary: A term, first used for San Francisco houses in a 1978 book, for Victorian and Edwardian houses repainted since the 1960s in three or more colours to highlight their details.

democratic-republican-party.name: Democratic-Republican Party
democratic-republican-party.summary: An American political party founded by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison in the 1790s, championing individual liberty and free trade, and dominant in politics after 1800.

federalist-party.name: Federalist Party
federalist-party.summary: The first American political party, dominating national government under Alexander Hamilton from 1789 to 1801 before declining after opposing the War of 1812.

gall-native-american-leader.name: Gall
gall-native-american-leader.summary: A Hunkpapa Lakota military leader (c.1840–1894) who fought at the Battle of the Little Bighorn, later lived in exile in Canada, and became a reservation judge advocating assimilation.

hunkpapa.name: Hunkpapa
hunkpapa.summary: One of the seven council fires of the Lakota Sioux, whose name means 'Head of the Circle,' referring to their traditional place at the entrance of the tribal council circle.

battle-of-the-little-bighorn.name: Battle of the Little Bighorn
battle-of-the-little-bighorn.summary: An 1876 battle in Montana in which Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho forces decisively defeated the U.S. 7th Cavalry, the most significant clash of the Great Sioux War.

7th-cavalry-regiment.name: 7th Cavalry
7th-cavalry-regiment.summary: A US Army cavalry regiment formed in 1866, famous for its defeat under Custer at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876 and its massacre of Lakota people at Wounded Knee.

john-borlase-warren.name: John Borlase Warren
john-borlase-warren.summary: Royal Navy officer, diplomat and politician (1753–1822) who also sat in the British House of Commons.

republic-of-texas.name: Republic of Texas
republic-of-texas.summary: A sovereign country in North America from 1836 to 1846, formed after the Texas Revolution against Mexico and later annexed by the United States.

nueces-river.name: Nueces River
nueces-river.summary: A roughly 315-mile river in Texas, named for the pecan trees along its banks, that Mexico claimed as its border with Texas before the Mexican-American War.

stephen-w-kearny.name: Stephen W. Kearny
stephen-w-kearny.summary: A US Army officer (1794–1848) known for his role in the Mexican–American War, especially the conquest of California, and for the Kearny Code governing New Mexico.

fort-leavenworth.name: Fort Leavenworth
fort-leavenworth.summary: A U.S. Army post in Kansas built in 1827, the second-oldest active Army post west of Washington, D.C., long a hub for westward expansion and now home to Army leadership training.

santa-fe-de-nuevo-m-xico.name: Santa Fe de Nuevo México
santa-fe-de-nuevo-m-xico.summary: A province of the Spanish Empire and later Mexico covering the area that became New Mexico, with its capital moved to Santa Fe in 1610.

alta-california.name: Alta California
alta-california.summary: Spanish then Mexican province established in 1804 covering present-day California, Nevada, Utah, and parts of neighboring states, ceded to the US after the Mexican-American War in 1848.

whitman-massacre.name: Whitman massacre
whitman-massacre.summary: The 1847 killing of missionaries Marcus and Narcissa Whitman and eleven others by Cayuse men who blamed Whitman for a measles epidemic, which spurred creation of the Oregon Territory.

cayuse-war.name: Cayuse War
cayuse-war.summary: An 1847-1855 conflict between the Cayuse people and American settlers, triggered by the Whitman massacre, which led to further wars in the Columbia Plateau region.

yakima-war.name: Yakama War
yakima-war.summary: An 1855–1858 conflict between the United States and the Yakama people and their allies in what is now Washington state.

puget-sound-war.name: Puget Sound War
puget-sound-war.summary: An armed conflict in 1855-56 in Washington's Puget Sound area between US forces and the Nisqually, Muckleshoot, Puyallup and Klickitat peoples, remembered for the Battle of Seattle and the execution of Chief Leschi.

leschi-nisqually.name: Chief Leschi
leschi-nisqually.summary: Chief of the Nisqually Tribe in Washington's Puget Sound (c. 1808-1858), hanged in 1858 for killing two territorial volunteers, though he was informally exonerated by Washington State in 2004.

napoleon.name: Napoleon
napoleon.summary: French emperor from 1804 to 1814, and briefly in 1815, who rose to power as a general during the French Revolution and led sweeping military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East.

arthur-wellesley-1st-duke-of-wellington.name: Duke of Wellington
arthur-wellesley-1st-duke-of-wellington.summary: British Army officer and statesman who served as Prime Minister and Commander-in-Chief, famed for defeating Napoleon's forces after rising through campaigns in India and the Peninsular War (1769–1852).

antonio-l-pez-de-santa-anna.name: Antonio López de Santa Anna
antonio-l-pez-de-santa-anna.summary: Mexican general and politician (1794–1876) who served as president of Mexico multiple times between 1833 and 1855, a dominant and controversial figure blamed for the loss of Mexican territory to the United States.

marcus-reno.name: Marcus Reno
marcus-reno.summary: U.S. Army officer who served under Custer and played a controversial role at the Battle of the Little Bighorn by holding a defensive position about 4 miles away rather than supporting Custer.

stephen-girard.name: Stephen Girard
stephen-girard.summary: A French-born American banker and philanthropist (1750–1831) who personally financed the US war effort during the War of 1812 and became one of the richest Americans in history.

john-neal.name: John Neal
john-neal.summary: American writer, critic and activist (1793–1876) who championed early American literary nationalism, advanced women's rights, and pioneered colloquial American prose style.

washington-irving.name: Washington Irving
washington-irving.summary: An early 19th-century American writer, essayist and diplomat known for the stories 'Rip Van Winkle' and 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow', and for historical works on Columbus, Muhammad and George Washington.

edgar-allan-poe.name: Edgar Allan Poe
edgar-allan-poe.summary: American writer (1809 to 1849) known for poetry and short stories of mystery and the macabre, regarded as a central figure of American Romanticism and Gothic fiction and a pioneer of detective fiction.

nathaniel-hawthorne.name: Nathaniel Hawthorne
nathaniel-hawthorne.summary: An American novelist and short-story writer (1804–1864) whose works, including The Scarlet Letter, explored history, morality and religion in New England.

the-scarlet-letter.name: The Scarlet Letter
the-scarlet-letter.summary: 1850 historical novel by Nathaniel Hawthorne set in Puritan Massachusetts, telling of Hester Prynne's punishment for adultery and her struggle toward dignity.

herman-melville.name: Herman Melville
herman-melville.summary: American writer (1819–1891) best known for Moby-Dick, whose reputation grew greatly only after a revival beginning around 1919.

moby-dick.name: Moby-Dick
moby-dick.summary: An 1851 novel by Herman Melville about Captain Ahab's pursuit of a giant white whale, now regarded as a Great American Novel though it sold poorly in its own time.

david-walker-abolitionist.name: David Walker
david-walker-abolitionist.summary: American abolitionist and writer (1796–1830) whose 1829 pamphlet, An Appeal to the Colored Citizens of the World, called for black unity against slavery.

frederick-douglass.name: Frederick Douglass
frederick-douglass.summary: American abolitionist, orator and writer who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became a leading 19th-century voice for African-American civil rights; his 1845 autobiography became a bestseller.

harriet-jacobs.name: Harriet Jacobs
harriet-jacobs.summary: African-American abolitionist and writer (1813 or 1815–1897) whose 1861 autobiography Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl recounted her escape from slavery.

incidents-in-the-life-of-a-slave-girl.name: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl
incidents-in-the-life-of-a-slave-girl.summary: 1861 autobiography by Harriet Jacobs describing her life as an enslaved woman and her efforts to gain freedom for herself and her children.
incidents-in-the-life-of-a-slave-girl.source_title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl

the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher.name: The Fall of the House of Usher
the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher.summary: Gothic short story by Edgar Allan Poe (1839) about madness and family decay, ending with a sister's revenge and the mansion's collapse; one of Poe's best-known works.
the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher.source_title: The Fall of the House of Usher

the-murders-in-the-rue-morgue.name: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
the-murders-in-the-rue-morgue.summary: Edgar Allan Poe's 1841 short story featuring detective C. Auguste Dupin, widely regarded as the first modern detective story.
the-murders-in-the-rue-morgue.source_title: The Murders in the Rue Morgue

victor-s-jour.name: Victor Séjour
victor-s-jour.summary: American writer born in New Orleans in 1817 who spent most of his career in Paris; his story 'Le Mulâtre' is the earliest known fiction by a Black American author.

le-mul-tre.name: Le Mulâtre
le-mul-tre.summary: A short story by Victor Séjour, written in French and published in Paris in 1837, considered the earliest known work of fiction by an African-American author.

paul-laurence-dunbar.name: Paul Laurence Dunbar
paul-laurence-dunbar.summary: American poet, novelist and short story writer (1872–1906), born to formerly enslaved parents, and one of the first African-American writers to gain international recognition.

gowongo-mohawk.name: Gowongo Mohawk
gowongo-mohawk.summary: A Seneca playwright and actor (1859–1924) who wrote and starred in her own successful play after being dissatisfied with the roles offered to Native American women.

seneca-people.name: Seneca
seneca-people.summary: An Iroquoian-speaking Indigenous nation that lived south of Lake Ontario and formed the westernmost of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee, known as 'Keepers of the Western Door.'

omar-ibn-said.name: Omar ibn Said
omar-ibn-said.summary: Enslaved Fula Muslim scholar (c. 1770–1864) taken from West Africa to the United States, who wrote Arabic-language works including an autobiography.

rachel-dyer.name: Rachel Dyer
rachel-dyer.summary: An 1828 Gothic novel by American writer John Neal, the first full-length novel about the Salem witch trials, which influenced later writers including Hawthorne and Whitman.

logan-novel.name: Logan
logan-novel.summary: An 1822 Gothic historical novel by American writer John Neal, loosely inspired by Mingo leader Logan the Orator, depicting colonist-Indigenous conflict on the Virginia frontier before the Revolutionary War.

seventy-six-novel.name: Seventy-Six
seventy-six-novel.summary: A historical novel about the American Revolutionary War, published in 1823 by John Neal, noted for its early use of colloquial American English and battle realism.

a-voyage-to-the-moon-tucker-novel.name: A Voyage to the Moon
a-voyage-to-the-moon-tucker-novel.summary: An 1827 satirical science fiction novel by George Tucker, one of the earliest American works in the genre, depicting a journey to two fictional lunar societies.
a-voyage-to-the-moon-tucker-novel.source_title: A Voyage to the Moon (Tucker novel)

e-pauline-johnson.name: E. Pauline Johnson
e-pauline-johnson.summary: Canadian Mohawk poet, author and performer (1861–1913) known by the stage name Tekahionwake, celebrated for blending Indigenous and English literary traditions in works like Flint and Feather and Legends of Vancouver.

low-countries.name: Low Countries
low-countries.summary: Historical lowland region of northwestern Europe roughly covering today's Belgium, Netherlands and Luxembourg, once one of the most densely populated and economically advanced parts of Europe.

rhineland.name: Rhineland
rhineland.summary: A loosely defined industrial region of western Germany along the Rhine, with historic ties to the Holy Roman Empire, Prussia, and the German Empire.

samuel-slater.name: Samuel Slater
samuel-slater.summary: English-American industrialist (1768–1835), called the 'Father of the American Industrial Revolution,' who brought British textile technology to the US and built its first textile mill.

eli-whitney.name: Eli Whitney
eli-whitney.summary: American inventor of the cotton gin in 1793, an invention that strengthened the economic foundation of slavery in the American South before his death in 1825.

cotton-gin.name: cotton gin
cotton-gin.summary: A machine that separates cotton fibers from seeds, modernized by Eli Whitney in 1793, which boosted US cotton production and, unintentionally, expanded the use of slave labor.

leuth-re-ir-n-e-du-pont.name: Éleuthère Irénée du Pont
leuth-re-ir-n-e-du-pont.summary: French-American chemist and industrialist (1771–1834) who founded the gunpowder maker E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company, starting the prominent du Pont family.

eleutherian-mills.name: Eleutherian Mills
eleutherian-mills.summary: A gunpowder mill site in Delaware used from 1802 to 1921, founded by Éleuthère Irénée du Pont, whose company grew into DuPont.

erie-canal.name: Erie Canal
erie-canal.summary: A canal completed in 1825 linking the Hudson River to Lake Erie, cutting transport costs across the Appalachians and speeding the growth of New York and the Great Lakes region.

douglas-irwin.name: Douglas Irwin
douglas-irwin.summary: Economist at Dartmouth College and expert on U.S. trade policy, especially during the Great Depression, who has written seven books.

andrew-johnson.name: Andrew Johnson
andrew-johnson.summary: 17th president of the United States (1865–1869), who succeeded Abraham Lincoln after his assassination and was later impeached, though acquitted by one Senate vote.

treaty-of-1818.name: Treaty of 1818
treaty-of-1818.summary: A treaty between the US and UK that also allowed joint occupation and settlement of the Oregon Country, marking Britain's last significant loss of territory in the continental United States.

oregon-country.name: Oregon Country
oregon-country.summary: A Pacific Northwest region jointly claimed by the UK and US after an 1818 treaty, until an 1846 treaty split it along the 49th parallel.

indian-removal-act.name: Indian Removal Act
indian-removal-act.summary: An 1830 US law signed by Andrew Jackson that forced over 60,000 American Indians from at least 18 tribes to relocate west of the Mississippi River, with many deaths along the way.

second-seminole-war.name: Second Seminole War
second-seminole-war.summary: A war from 1835 to 1842 in Florida between the United States and Seminole groups, the longest and costliest of the US Indian conflicts.

james-monroe.name: James Monroe
james-monroe.summary: Fifth U.S. president (1817–1825) and Founding Father who issued the Monroe Doctrine opposing European colonialism in the Americas.

monroe-doctrine.name: Monroe Doctrine
monroe-doctrine.summary: A US foreign policy declared by President James Monroe in 1823 opposing European interference in the Americas, later used to justify American dominance across the hemisphere.

manifest-destiny.name: Manifest destiny
manifest-destiny.summary: A 19th-century American belief that settlers were destined to expand westward across North America, rooted in ideas of moral and national superiority and used to justify territorial expansion.

uss-boston-1884.name: USS Boston
uss-boston-1884.summary: A US Navy protected cruiser commissioned in the 1880s, among the first steel warships of the 'New Navy,' whose landed marines helped depose Hawaii's Queen Lili'uokalani in 1893.

lili-uokalani.name: Liliʻuokalani
lili-uokalani.summary: Last sovereign monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, reigning 1891–1893 until overthrown in a coup; composed the song "Aloha ʻOe" and wrote her autobiography while imprisoned.

kal-kaua.name: Kalākaua
kal-kaua.summary: Last king of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, reigning from 1874 to 1891, nicknamed the 'Merrie Monarch' for reviving the hula, and known for a world tour and lavish spending.

rupert-s-land.name: Rupert's Land
rupert-s-land.summary: A territory in British North America based on the Hudson Bay drainage basin, granted to the Hudson's Bay Company for trade from 1670 to 1870, covering much of present-day Canada.

hudson-s-bay-company.name: Hudson's Bay Company
hudson-s-bay-company.summary: A Canadian company founded in 1670 that controlled the North American fur trade and acted as the de facto government of British North America until 1869, later becoming a department store chain before liquidating in 2025.

northwest-territories.name: Northwest Territories
northwest-territories.summary: A territory of northern Canada formed in 1870 on lands of the Dene and Inuvialuit peoples, with Yellowknife as its capital since 1967.

trail-of-tears.name: Trail of Tears
trail-of-tears.summary: The forced displacement of about 60,000 Native Americans of the Five Civilized Tribes between 1830 and 1850, during which many died of exposure, disease and starvation.

five-civilized-tribes.name: Five Civilized Tribes
five-civilized-tribes.summary: A US government term for five Native American nations in the Southeast—the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee and Seminole—seen as having adopted Anglo-American culture before their forced removal.

thirteenth-amendment-to-the-united-state.name: Thirteenth Amendment
thirteenth-amendment-to-the-united-state.summary: The US constitutional amendment outlawing slavery and involuntary servitude except as criminal punishment, ratified in December 1865 as the first of three Reconstruction Amendments.
thirteenth-amendment-to-the-united-state.source_title: Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

forty-eighters.name: Forty-eighters
forty-eighters.summary: Europeans, many German, who took part in the 1848 revolutions and emigrated abroad, often to the US, after their defeat.

carl-schurz.name: Carl Schurz
carl-schurz.summary: German-American revolutionary turned American statesman (1829–1906) who fought in the 1848–49 German revolutions, served as a Union general, and later became U.S. Secretary of the Interior.

fritz-anneke.name: Fritz Anneke
fritz-anneke.summary: German revolutionary and journalist (1818-1872) who emigrated to the US in 1849 and served as a Union Army officer in the Civil War.

joseph-weydemeyer.name: Joseph Weydemeyer
joseph-weydemeyer.summary: Prussian-born military officer, journalist and Marxist revolutionary who became a follower of Marx and Engels, emigrated to the U.S. in 1851, and served as a Union Army officer.

american-colonization-society.name: American Colonization Society
american-colonization-society.summary: An organization founded in 1816 to resettle free and formerly enslaved Black Americans in West Africa, leading to the founding of Liberia.

washington-territory.name: Washington Territory
washington-territory.summary: A US territory from 1853 to 1889 carved from Oregon Territory, at its largest including present-day Idaho and parts of Montana and Wyoming, before becoming the State of Washington.

arctic-archipelago.name: Arctic Archipelago
arctic-archipelago.summary: A group of over 36,000 islands north of mainland Canada, also called the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, covering about 1.4 million square kilometres in Nunavut and the Northwest Territories.

william-james.name: William James
william-james.summary: American philosopher and psychologist (1842–1910), the first to teach a psychology course in the US, dubbed the 'father of American psychology', and co-founder of pragmatism with Charles Sanders Peirce.

ralph-waldo-emerson.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
ralph-waldo-emerson.summary: American essayist, lecturer and philosopher (1803–1882) who led the transcendentalist movement and was seen as a champion of individualism and critical thinking.

pragmatism.name: Pragmatism
pragmatism.summary: A philosophical tradition, begun in the United States in the 1870s, that treats thought and language as tools for solving problems and predicting outcomes rather than mirroring reality.

transcendentalism.name: Transcendentalism
transcendentalism.summary: An American philosophical and literary movement of the late 1820s and 1830s holding that people and nature are inherently good, prizing intuitive individual insight over strict empiricism.

henry-david-thoreau.name: Henry David Thoreau
henry-david-thoreau.summary: American naturalist, essayist, and philosopher (1817 to 1862), a leading transcendentalist best known for Walden and the essay "Civil Disobedience."

unitarianism.name: Unitarianism
unitarianism.summary: A nontrinitarian Christian movement holding that God is a single being rather than a Trinity, viewing Jesus as an inspired moral teacher rather than equal to God.

alexander-h-stephens.name: Alexander Stephens
alexander-h-stephens.summary: An American politician (1812-1883) who served as the only vice president of the Confederate States and later as Georgia's governor, having backed slavery's expansion before the Civil War.

cornerstone-speech.name: Cornerstone Speech
cornerstone-speech.summary: An 1861 speech by Confederate acting Vice President Alexander H. Stephens in Savannah, delivered just before the Civil War, defending slavery as the basis of the Confederacy.

josiah-royce.name: Josiah Royce
josiah-royce.summary: American philosopher (1855–1916) and founder of American idealism, known for combining pragmatism with idealism and for his philosophy of loyalty.

ghost-dance.name: Ghost Dance
ghost-dance.summary: A ceremony begun in 1889 by Northern Paiute leader Wovoka, believed to reunite the living with the dead and bring peace; it spread widely and shaped Lakota resistance.

paiute.name: Paiute
paiute.summary: A historical label for three related but distinct Indigenous peoples of the Great Basin in the western United States, speaking related but separate Numic languages.

lakota-people.name: Lakota
lakota-people.summary: A Native American people, also called the Teton Sioux, who moved onto the northern Great Plains in the 17th century and made the Black Hills their spiritual center by the 1770s.

sitting-bull.name: Sitting Bull
sitting-bull.summary: A Hunkpapa Lakota leader (c. 1831–1890) who led resistance against U.S. government policies and whose vision preceded the Lakota victory at Little Bighorn; he was killed in 1890 during an arrest attempt.

wounded-knee-massacre.name: Wounded Knee Massacre
wounded-knee-massacre.summary: An 1890 conflict in which the US Army killed between 250 and 300 Lakota people near Wounded Knee Creek, South Dakota, after trying to disarm them.

scottish-common-sense-realism.name: Scottish common sense realism
scottish-common-sense-realism.summary: A school of philosophy founded by Scottish thinkers such as Thomas Reid during the 18th-century Scottish Enlightenment, holding that common sense is the foundation of philosophical inquiry; it opposed David Hume and influenced late 18th-century America.

john-locke.name: John Locke
john-locke.summary: English Enlightenment philosopher and physician, called the father of liberalism, whose writings on toleration and government by consent of the governed influenced the American Declaration of Independence.

thomas-brown-philosopher.name: Thomas Brown
thomas-brown-philosopher.summary: A Scottish physician, philosopher and poet (1778–1820) who held the Chair of Moral Philosophy at Edinburgh University from 1810 to 1820.

william-paley.name: William Paley
william-paley.summary: English Anglican clergyman and philosopher (1743–1805) best known for his 1802 teleological argument for God's existence using the watchmaker analogy.

dugald-stewart.name: Dugald Stewart
dugald-stewart.summary: A Scottish philosopher and mathematician (1753–1828), a leading later Scottish Enlightenment figure who popularized the ideas of Francis Hutcheson and Adam Smith through his Edinburgh lectures.

charles-sanders-peirce.name: Charles Sanders Peirce
charles-sanders-peirce.summary: American scientist, mathematician, logician and philosopher (1839–1914), sometimes called 'the father of pragmatism' and described by admirers as America's greatest logician.

johns-hopkins-university.name: Johns Hopkins University
johns-hopkins-university.summary: Private research university in Baltimore, incorporated in 1867, considered the first research university in the US, funded by a bequest from philanthropist Johns Hopkins.

journal-of-speculative-philosophy.name: Journal of Speculative Philosophy
journal-of-speculative-philosophy.summary: American academic journal examining philosophical questions and the relevance of past philosophers to modern thought, published quarterly by Penn State University Press.

george-fitzhugh.name: George Fitzhugh
george-fitzhugh.summary: American social theorist (1806–1881) and leading pro-slavery intellectual before the Civil War, who argued slavery was more humane and stable than Northern capitalism.

thomas-carlyle.name: Thomas Carlyle
thomas-carlyle.summary: A Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher (1795–1881), known as the 'sage of Chelsea,' whose writings, including The French Revolution: A History, strongly shaped Victorian intellectual culture.

benjamin-franklin.name: Benjamin Franklin
benjamin-franklin.summary: American polymath, printer and Founding Father (1706–1790) who signed the Declaration of Independence and served as the first postmaster general.

adam-smith.name: Adam Smith
adam-smith.summary: Scottish economist and philosopher (1723–1790), a pioneer of political economy often called the 'father of economics,' best known for The Wealth of Nations and The Theory of Moral Sentiments.

albert-taylor-bledsoe.name: Albert Taylor Bledsoe
albert-taylor-bledsoe.summary: American Confederate officer, priest and professor (1809–1877) known for his 1856 book Liberty and Slavery, an extensive defense of slavery, and later as an architect of the Lost Cause narrative.

lost-cause-of-the-confederacy.name: Lost Cause of the Confederacy
lost-cause-of-the-confederacy.summary: A pseudohistorical myth, first articulated in 1866, claiming the Confederacy's cause in the Civil War was just and not centered on slavery; it shaped Southern racial attitudes into the 21st century.

james-henley-thornwell.name: James Henley Thornwell
james-henley-thornwell.summary: American Presbyterian preacher and slaveowner from South Carolina (1812–1862) who supported the Confederacy while unusually arguing enslaved people were made in God's image.

second-great-awakening.name: Second Great Awakening
second-great-awakening.summary: A religious revival in the late 18th and early 19th century United States that spread evangelical Protestantism through emotional preaching, sparked new denominations, and fueled reform movements including abolitionism.

native-american-church.name: Native American Church
native-american-church.summary: Syncretic Native American religion combining traditional beliefs with elements of Christianity and the sacramental use of peyote, originating in Oklahoma Territory in the late 19th century; today the most widespread indigenous religion among Native Americans.

oklahoma-territory.name: Oklahoma Territory
oklahoma-territory.summary: A US territory from 1890 to 1907, formed from the western half of Indian Territory and a strip north of Texas, later joined to become the state of Oklahoma.

victor-griffin-quapaw.name: Victor Griffin
victor-griffin-quapaw.summary: Elected chief of the Quapaw Tribe of Indians (c. 1873–1958) and a peyote roadman who helped spread the Native American Church among several tribes; he conferred with every U.S. president during his term as chief.

quapaw.name: Quapaw
quapaw.summary: Federally recognized Native American tribe, also called the Ogáxpa or "Downstream" people, whose ancestral homelands spanned from the Ohio River to Arkansas before forced removal in 1834.

great-spirit.name: Great Spirit
great-spirit.summary: A supreme being or life force in the traditional religious beliefs of many Indigenous cultures in Canada and the United States, known by different names such as Wakan Tanka and Gitche Manitou.

prince-maximilian-of-wied-neuwied.name: Prince Maximilian of Wied-Neuwied
prince-maximilian-of-wied-neuwied.summary: Prince Maximilian of Wied-Neuwied: A German explorer, ethnologist and naturalist who led expeditions to Brazil from 1815 to 1817 and to the United States starting in 1832, the latter with painter Karl Bodmer.

karl-bodmer.name: Karl Bodmer
karl-bodmer.summary: Swiss-French printmaker and painter (1809-1893) best known in the United States for accurate paintings of the American frontier, made while accompanying explorer Maximilian zu Wied-Neuwied's 1832-1834 Missouri River expedition.

choctaw.name: Choctaw
choctaw.summary: An Indigenous people of the Southeastern Woodlands of the United States, historically based in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama, today enrolled in three federally recognized tribes.

cherokee.name: Cherokee
cherokee.summary: Indigenous people of the Southeastern Woodlands of the United States, historically concentrated in the Carolinas, Georgia, Tennessee and Alabama; by the 19th century settlers classified them as one of the 'Five Civilized Tribes.'

blood-quantum-laws.name: blood quantum laws
blood-quantum-laws.summary: US federal and state laws, first imposed in the 18th century, that define Native American identity by fractions of ancestry; many tribes do not use this measure themselves.

buffalo-bill.name: Buffalo Bill
buffalo-bill.summary: American soldier, bison hunter and showman (1846–1917) who founded Buffalo Bill's Wild West in 1883, touring shows about the frontier and Indian Wars across the US and, from 1887, Europe.

edward-two-two.name: Edward Two-Two
edward-two-two.summary: Lakota Sioux performer (c.1851–1914) who appeared at Hagenbeck in Hamburg and the Sarrasani circus in Dresden, presenting Native American life to German audiences.

sarrasani.name: Sarrasani
sarrasani.summary: A German circus company founded in Dresden in 1901 that became one of Europe's largest circuses in the early 20th century, before its theatre was destroyed in the 1945 bombing of Dresden.
